contagion19.text_read: abstract (EconPapers, VoR) + full text of working-paper version (CESifo WP 8263, April 2020); VoR full text not read
key_findings: "we find that anti-social behavior is generally more contagious than pro-social behavior." (abstract)
"social proximity amplifies the contagion of anti-social behavior more strongly than the contagion of pro-social behavior." (abstract)
"Anti-social individuals are also most susceptible to the behavioral contagion of other anti-social peers." (abstract)

WP design: 185 active participants, 9 lab sessions, BaER-Lab Paderborn; give-or-take game with a charity (EUR 15); proximity = peer described as more vs less similar (25 dating-site questions); unknown/high/low treatments

WP: frequency of contagion 33.7% after anti-social vs 19.4% after pro-social observation (p=0.027); in non-high proximity conditions contagion "is less frequent and not significantly different between the types of observed behavior" (Sec. 3.3) [numbers from WP via fetch summary, re-check against VoR before quoting]

metadata_corrections.authors: Eugen Dimant (sole author) - confirmed; NOT coauthored. (The coauthored Dimant, Gelfand, Hochleitner & Sonderegger paper 'Strategic Behavior with Tight, Loose and Polarized Norms' is a different paper, CESifo WP 10233 / Management Science 2025.)

key_findings: "Existing methods focus on measuring norms in the form of what the average or most frequent behavior/opinion is in a given context."
"The complementary method presented here offers the ability to measure the distribution of norm-related beliefs at the individual level in an incentive-compatible way,"
"This approach intuitively captures the tightness and looseness of norms, addressing scenarios where mean or modal outcomes may conceal underlying variations."
"This paper is accompanied by ready-made Qualtrics software"

biz14.evidence: Anderson 2003 abstract: individuals avoid decisions by "postponing them, failing to act, or accepting the status quo"; status quo bias is one of the 4 effects.

judg08.evidence: Anderson 2003 abstract lists choice deferral among the 4 decision-avoidance effects.

judg01.evidence: K&T 1979 abstract: "value is assigned to gains and losses rather than to final assets"

issues: Boundary correct: the fixed ~2:1 (2.25) coefficient comes from Tversky & Kahneman 1992, not the 1979 paper.
judg07.evidence: K&T 1979 abstract: "value is assigned to gains and losses rather than to final assets"; value function "is generally steeper for losses than for gains"

issues: Option 0 ('Loss aversion can reverse in experiments') rests on a contested result: André & de Langhe (2021, JEP:General 150(12), 2659-2665) argue the reversal is a measurement artifact (different lotteries per condition) and vanishes when only common lotteries are analyzed. The answer key presents it as settled.
Original abstract claim itself is accurately paraphrased.

corrections.options[0]: Measured loss aversion shifted with the range of gains and losses shown
corrections.explain: Walasek & Stewart (2015) reported that measured loss aversion disappeared or reversed when the range of gains and losses changed; a reanalysis (André & de Langhe, 2021) argued this reflects different lotteries across conditions, so the reversal is contested.
corrections.boundary: This does not imply that loss aversion is never observed, and the reversal finding itself has been challenged.

judg02.evidence: W&S 2015 abstract: "We were able to find loss aversion, loss neutrality, and even the reverse of loss aversion." André & de Langhe 2021 abstract: "analyzing only the subset of lotteries that are common across conditions eliminates the pattern of results."

issues: Scene misdescribes the design: not a workplace collaboration study; five preregistered studies (15 behavioral experiments, >8,600 participants) on Trump supporters vs opponents.

corrections.scene: Across a series of online experiments, Trump supporters and opponents report feeling closer to their own side and also make costly choices toward the other side.

social18.evidence: Abstract: "anti-social behavior is generally more contagious than pro-social behavior."

issues: Scene contrasts a close colleague with 'a stranger'; the design contrasted an anonymous peer described as more vs less similar (high vs low proximity), with an unknown-proximity control. All peers were anonymous.

corrections.scene: A team member sees an antisocial act by a colleague they know is similar to them rather than one who is dissimilar.

social19.evidence: Abstract: "social proximity amplifies the contagion of anti-social behavior more strongly than the contagion of pro-social behavior." WP 8263: high/low treatments told participants whether the observed peer was more or less similar than a second peer.

social20.evidence: Abstract: method measures "the distribution of norm-related beliefs at the individual level", "addressing scenarios where mean or modal outcomes may conceal underlying variations"; title names polarization.

issues: Option 0 wording ('How many different normative positions') slightly mischaracterizes the method, which elicits the shape/spread of the belief distribution, not a count. Suggested tweak only.

corrections.options[0]: How spread out (tight, loose or polarized) do they perceive views to be?
